summary:
Yukon is a territory of Canada. Its human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression among prohibited grounds of discrimination, covering employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Legal change of gender is available in Yukon. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates fall under territorial jurisdiction; the sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a marker.

On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with members rising to speak across party lines. Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised the courage, resilience, contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledged that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of suicide attempt. This is the territory's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents on record.

On 13 June 2024 Yukon News reported that a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend in June 2024, with a replacement flag promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123).

Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (published 30 March 2026) reports that police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and up 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and up 184% since 2020. These are national figures; the release does not report Yukon-level victimisation. Police-reported hate crime rates are about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), which bears on sparsely-populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines police-reported hate-crime data with gender identity or expression and sexual-orientation motivations; its figures are national and do not report Yukon-level victimisation.
tangentialFactors:
The national hate-crime statistics cited above are national aggregates and do not measure Yukon specifically; the metropolitan-versus-smaller-town gap in reporting rates suggests that police-reported figures for a sparsely-populated territory may understate incidence.

The 2020 Privy Council Office poll found 87.6% of respondents said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour — a national attitudinal snapshot, not a Yukon-specific measure.

The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologised in December 2020 for institutional bias and pledged to stand against transphobia through an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee; this is a national policing commitment rather than a Yukon-specific one.
localsOnly:
Adoption by same-sex couples was legalised in Yukon in 2003 as part of nationwide legalisation.

Yukon's SOGI 123 policy governs sexual orientation and gender identity in territorial schools; the Education Minister publicly reaffirmed it in June 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a gender marker on a birth certificate or other vital-statistics document; this remains unresolved in this record.

No Yukon-specific hate-crime or victimisation figures are available in the sources; the Statistics Canada and Egale Canada data are national.

No documented instance of trans-specific violence in Yukon appears in the sources; the most recent documented incident in this record is the June 2024 Pride flag vandalism at a Whitehorse school, and no later instance is documented.
